Thus, every time after analyzing the established state of affairs and alignment of
forces, Lenin determines, firstly, with specific further steps towards achieving
immediate goals and, secondly, with an assessment of the strategic perspective
of the development of the situation as a whole.
That is why each such article turns out to be not just a beautiful dialectical twist
(decorative icon), but a guide to action; each of his articles contains a
description of a way out of the current situation and a transition (possibly with a
leap) to a new turn-level of development of interacting elements, and in each
article without exception the author offers his original and effective solution to
the problem under consideration.
All of Lenin's forecasts are made on the basis of correctly composed relations
from interacting sides-components of reality and also based on anticipating the
trend or orientation of subsequent contentful filling of these relations. At the
same time, the more accurately the sides-components directly opposing,
confronting and interacting with each other are identified, the more correct and
reliable the predictions of further development of events and situations turn out
to be.
Of course, conditions, circumstances and forms interacting in the present differ
from those of the past, but the principle (algorithm, "mechanism") determining
the development of reality is invariant over time; that is why the proposed
scheme or methodology of effective research into the surrounding world
resembles the one presented above.
Below we will analyze all this using examples of well-known theoretical works by
V.I. Lenin relating to three different periods of his life: pre-revolutionary,
immediate pre-revolutionary and post-revolutionary.

§ 1. Works of the pre-revolutionary period
We will examine the dialectical background of Lenin's works from the prerevolutionary period (which began a dozen and a half years before the Great
October Socialist Revolution) using such Leninist works as “What Is to Be
Done?”, “One Step Forward, Two Steps Back”, “The Beginning of the Revolution
in Russia”, “Marxism and Revisionism” and “On the Road”, united by a single
internal logic and canvas of corresponding historical events.
1. In his book “What Is to Be Done? Burning Questions of Our Movement” [8,
pp. 80–236], published in March 1902, Lenin presented an overview of the initial
stage of the revolutionary movement in Russia. The book was written during the

 acute struggle for the creation of a revolutionary Marxist party of the Russian
working class and played an outstanding role in the formation of the party.
In this work, Lenin identifies three stages and accordingly — three periods in the
development of the revolutionary movement in Russia.
He describes the first stage of 1884–1894 as the embryonic development of
social democracy carried out separately from the labor movement.
Regarding the second stage of 1894–1898: "social-democracy appears on earth
as a public movement, as an upsurge of popular masses, as a political party" [8,
p. 227]. Alongside and instead of "going into the people", there began a flow of
intelligentsia toward workers (as the most active force-component of the future
revolutionary movement) and widespread fascination among workers with
strikes. However, this same strike struggle for the sake of increasing its own
efficiency forced them to learn, read illegal literature, as well as diligently engage
with issues of legal populism without forgetting at the same time about Marxist
theory and the task of overthrowing autocracy. "The establishment of the party
in the spring of 1898 was the most vivid and at the same time last act of the
Social Democrats of this stripe" [8, p. 228].
The third stage finally replaces the second one starting in 1898. It is a period of
confusion, vacillation, disintegration. The leaders of the movement were afraid to
move forward (to political struggle), yielding to the strength of the spontaneous
upsurge of the popular masses. The slogan "class struggle" did not push towards
ever broader, more energetic activity but served as a means of appeasement:
after all, everyone knows that "economic struggle is inextricably linked with
political". The idea of the party did not serve as a call to create a combat
organization of revolutionaries but justified some kind of "revolutionary
bureaucracy", childish playing with "democratic" forms. And here, in this
connection, the author, like a true scholar drawing conclusions only based on
facts (without fabrications or fantasies), having difficulty saying when the third
stage will end and the fourth begin, nevertheless expresses firm confidence that
the fourth stage will lead to strengthening militant Marxism; that the rear-guard
of conciliators and deserters will be replaced by the actual vanguard of the most
revolutionary class (proletariat), which will manage to overcome uncertainty,
hesitation and lack of confidence in their own forces. And then (in terms of
calling for such a change and summarizing what has been said), it becomes
possible to give a concise and exhaustive answer to the question "what is to be
done?" — liquidate the third stage (period of confusion, vacillations, hesitations
and lack of confidence in one's own forces) [8, p. 229].
[Thus, Lenin outlined here the objectively occurring successive replacement of
stages (forms) of substantive revolutionary movement expressed qualitatively
and quantitatively through changes in the correlation between the contentful and
formal components in the known relation {proletariat/bourgeoisie}. The
correlation of components (within the specified relation) changes with the growth
in share and importance of the active revolutionary component (proletariat) due

 to increased contentfulness conditioned by the influence of the following
accompanying factors: emergence of social democracy => becoming established
of social democracy => unification of social democratic formations on the basis
of the idea of creating a Marxist proletarian party => establishment of the
Bolshevik Party of the Russian working class as its most revolutionary vanguard.
This entire chain of transforming factors directly affected the numerator of the
aforementioned relation (i.e., the "proletariat" component), raising
its contentfulness within the whole relation.
In other words, Vladimir Ilyich, with impartiality of a scientist, stated that for the
period from 1884 to 1898 and further (later) there took place and continues
objective
movement
(transformation,
transmutation)
of
the contentful component of the mentioned relation towards increasing
its contentfulness while simultaneously upsetting equilibrium in the relation
{proletariat/bourgeoisie} in favor of strengthening and predominance of
influence of more contentful active proletarian forms of movement over more
conservative bourgeois ones. An innate ability and predisposition for dialectical
thinking allowed Vladimir Ilyich to break down step-by-step the phase-wise and
periodic nature of the revolutionary struggle, identify the active and passive
forces-components of the revolutionary movement in Russia of that time, trace
their genesis and determine measures to activate and strengthen

There is also a source of replenishment of the contentfulness of the "proletariat"

2. The continuation of the struggle for cleansing the revolutionary movement
and its vanguard (the Marxist party) from its wavering members (random
elements) is described very vividly by Lenin in the book “One Step Forward,
Two Steps Back (Crisis in Our Party)” [8, pp. 237–421]. The book resulted
from Lenin's thorough study and analysis of numerous protocols of meetings and
resolutions of the II Congress of the RSDLP and was released in May 1904. In
this work, Vladimir Ilyich shows how something big, main and essential
eventually emerges and takes shape from small things (seemingly insignificant
matters, squabbles, disputes, discussions and quarrels serving as signs of fierce
clash of opinions and different points of view). The art of a great dialectician
manifested itself in this case in recognizing this essential thing — the role and
significance of organizational issues in the process of forming the core of the
revolutionary movement (i.e., the Bolshevik Party), as well as timely
demarcation from conciliators and wavering elements regarding principal
questions, attracting to one's side by polemic and persuasion the majority of
potential sympathizers. As a result of this struggle, the idea emerged of
establishing and organizing a monolithic nucleus of the labor movement — the
Bolshevik Party — in opposition to amateurishness and circle-mindedness
characteristic of the social-democratic movement. Without consolidation around
a single center, without subordination to decisions of this center (that is, without

 iron discipline), the future conquests of the Great October would have simply
been unthinkable and impossible. Precisely from the standpoint of the dialectical
approach (from beginning to end), Lenin conducts his painstaking analysis of the
accompanying events of this struggle. For the proletariat (and any public
association alike) there is no other weapon in the struggle for power
except organization (organized effort) — writes Lenin. The proletariat can
become an invincible force only because the ideological unity of its theoretical
principles (first of all, Marxist theory) is secured by material unity of organization
uniting millions of workers into a single army (of the working class). Before this
army, the decrepit power of international capital will not stand. This army will
draw closer and tighter ranks despite any zigzags and steps backward [8, p.
413].
In the course of detailed study of the background of this issue, Lenin draws
attention to the fact that every development indeed proceeds along a dialectical
path of resolving emerging contradictions: minority becomes majority, majority
becomes minority, each side moves from defense to attack and from attack to
defense; the original point of ideological struggle is "negated", but then begins
"negation of negation" and the struggling sides return to the original point of
purely ideological struggle, but now this "thesis" is enriched by all the results of
the "antithesis" and turns into a higher "synthesis"; when an isolated random
error has grown into a quasi-system of conciliatory views on the organizational
issue, and the erroneousness of such an approach becomes increasingly
apparent. "In short, not only oats grow according to Hegel, but Russian socialdemocrats fight among themselves too according to Hegel," concludes Vladimir
Ilyich [8, p. 410].
[It is extremely important to note that the dialectical character of formulating
various conclusions and findings through "piling up" and layering of minor
questions and discussion results upon each other or through "returning to
oneself at a new level" is recorded by the author as self-evident.
Of course, for us living today, concepts and terms like "proletariat",
"bourgeoisie", "classes", "class struggle", etc., seem antiquated and exotic. At
the same time, forgetting the terminology of the past does not mean liberation
from the elements of developing reality denoted by it. After all, the class
structure of society still persists, whatever anyone says: on the one hand —
hired labor, on the other — financial-industrial capital (generally speaking,
"oligarchy"). And only the most shameless liar risks claiming that everything in
such a public arrangement is "even". That is why the meaning of the phrase
"class struggle" nowadays differs little from the content of this terminology in the
examined pre-revolutionary times, and the concept of "class struggle" is unlikely
to disappear until the notion of "classes" fades away. Therefore, even today it
remains important (and perhaps even more so) to be able to find interacting
components (competing, conflicting, confronting sides) and correctly compose
relevant content-form relations (of the type {content/form}) in order to properly
define directions of variability both of the components themselves and of their
relations as a whole (i.e., of social systems and structures), distinguish and

 separate the essential from the secondary (less significant) and thereby predict
changes in existing forms and the appearance of new ones. All this, undoubtedly,
may assist in devising the most effective forms of class struggle, etc. Applying to

owners of means of production}, etc., without loss of meaning. Our current

It is enough to look more closely to see the same standard scheme serving

events of Bloody Sunday in St. Petersburg. Judging by the fact that the
spring was slowly compressing ("the tsarist government deliberately gave
relatively unhindered development to strike movements and the beginnings
of broad demonstrations"), it was not difficult to assume that the
government acted with the intention of driving things toward the use of
military force [8, p. 422]. As a result: thousands killed and wounded. The
Rubicon has been crossed: the compressed-to-the-limit spring had to release
its accumulated energy — the proletariat rose up and began to arm itself.
And immediately the entire palette of revolutionary appeals, slogans and
actions changes. The rebellious Petrograd workers put forward demands for
immediate convocation of a constituent assembly based on universal, direct,
equal and secret suffrage, as well as for the immediate overthrow of the
government; at the same time, "arming the people becomes one of the
nearest tasks of the revolutionary moment." Events develop with astonishing
speed: "the revolutionary education of the proletariat advanced in one day

 more than it could have done in months and years of gray, humdrum,
downtrodden life". Immediate arming of workers and all citizens generally (it
was recognized and pointed out that revolutionaries of bourgeois democracy
could be used for the overthrow of Tsarism), "preparation and organization of
revolutionary forces for the destruction of governmental authorities and
institutions — this is the practical basis upon which all and any
revolutionaries can and should combine for a common blow" [8, p. 424].
[It should be noted here that there are no Councils of Workers', Soldiers' or
Peasants' Deputies yet on the forefront of the growing struggle. The situation
develops exclusively within the framework of the relation composed
("formed") of directly interacting components {proletariat/autocracy}: on the
one side — the working class under the wing of the Social-Democratic Party;
on the other side — autocracy with its coercive institutions].
And no matter how the present uprising ends in St. Petersburg itself, it will
inevitably and necessarily become the first step toward a much broader,
more conscious, better-prepared uprising. The government may manage to
postpone the hour of reckoning, but postponement will only make the next
step of the revolutionary onslaught even grander [8, p. 423].
[This example clearly demonstrates how V.I. Lenin masterfully formulated
and "calibrated" the previously reproduced dialectical scheme: precise
identification and definition of interacting constituents-components in their
relation {organizing proletariat/institutions of autocratic power}; identifying
the active component in this relation; determining the direction of variability
(movement, development) of the active component and the whole relation;
forecasting the emergence, accordingly, of new contentful forms as a result
of this change-movement.
Human thought always tends towards representing (expressing) its most
perfect form of maximum content volume. Structurally-compositionally, the
same scheme looks like this: description of the established situation in
conditions of disequilibrium; identification of causes and backgrounds
contributing to disruption of situational equilibrium; description of the
process of situation development while moving it towards a more
equilibrated, more balanced state; description of the new state of affairs and
newly emerging situation replacing the existing one due to inevitable ongoing
changes].
4. The article "Marxism and Revisionism" [8, pp. 36–43] was written in
March-April 1908. Describing the initial starting position, Lenin draws attention to
the alignment of forces (i.e., lists interacting components) in the course of the
struggle unfolding in the theoretical sphere. In this sphere, newly emerged
natural-historical theories in the mid-19th century, touching old theological
prejudices, caused and continue to cause the fiercest opposition and struggle [8,
p. 36]. Bourgeois scientific thought and philosophy do not want to hear anything
about Marxism, declaring it refuted and destroyed [how wonderfully "fresh" and

 recognizable is such an attitude toward Marxism even today!]. The increasing
role of Marxism and consolidation of its ideas among the working class inevitably
provokes sharpening bourgeois attacks against Marxism, which after each
"destruction" by official science becomes stronger, tougher and livelier. Having
defeated and outplayed many hostile external currents over the past fifty years,
today Marxism faces opposing currents requiring its correction within Marxism
itself. Pre-Marxian socialism remains strong in Russia and sometimes revives.
Generally speaking, pre-Marxian socialism has been broken, but it continues
fighting not on its own independent ground but on common Marxist ground — as
revisionism [trying to legalize and prove viability of a mixture of "a bulldog with
a rhinoceros"]. Essentially, however, all this petty-bourgeois revision of Marxism
(revision of small shopkeepers) always boils down to negation or diminution of
the factor of class struggle and channeling class struggle into the stream of
"class cooperation" [8, pp. 38–39].
What accounts for the inevitability of periodic revival of revisionism and its roots
under capitalism? It lies in the fact that in any capitalist country there are always
broad layers of petty bourgeoisie, small proprietors alongside the proletariat.
Capitalism was born and constantly reborn (regenerated) from small production
[8, p. 42]! A whole series of "middle strata" [by analogy with some "middle
class", using modern language] is inevitably created again and again by
capitalism due to its inner necessity (services of individual craftsmen, homebased work, small workshops serving large industry, etc.). When they go
bankrupt, these small producers are inevitably thrown back into the ranks of the
proletariat, "diluting" their views and beliefs with petty-bourgeois worldview,
their ideology (which, apparently, requires constant work on retraining and reeducation). This is completely natural and will be so for a long time while
antagonistic classes exist. And ideological struggle of revolutionary Marxism with
revisionism is merely the prelude to great revolutionary battles of the proletariat
until complete victory of its cause despite all vacillations and weaknesses of the
petit bourgeoisie [8, p. 43].
Bypassing superficial phenomena (effects), Lenin constantly brings to light the
most essential, profound sides-components consisting in actual relations of
interaction and confrontation. Thus, contrary to the widespread opinion among
revisionists, he states that growing parliamentarism and education of the
proletariat do not weaken crises and eliminate revolutions but, on the contrary,
contribute to intensifying civil war during these crises and revolutions [8, p. 41].
They (parliamentarism and education) help enlighten and organize ever larger
masses of population correspondingly to the increase ("piling up") of substantive
(informational) accumulations. This constitutes the internal dialectics of
parliamentarism and bourgeois democratism, subordinate following of which
expresses itself in even more acute than before resolution of disputes and
contradictions through mass violence.
[Lenin is a master at identifying dialectically confronting components (i.e., the
most interconnected and substantially conflicting sides, speaking in everyday
terms) in all episodes of development of reality that he analyzes. In this case,

 according to the established circumstances, he identifies the main actively
interacting components of development (of the revolutionary movement):
Bolsheviks on one side, Mensheviks on the other. Ideological grounds or
background guiding the interacting parties are: revolutionary Marxism on the
one hand, and revisionism on the other. Material carriers of these sides turn out
to be the revolutionary proletariat on one side and wavering petty-bourgeois
middling elements on the other. At later times, the latter would give way to
bourgeois intelligentsia (unsteady, eternally vacillating and conciliatory). Then
Lenin identifies the active contentful component, anticipates the direction of its
change-movement, and further forecasts the orientation and priority of
subsequent movement-development of the entire system composed of the
considered components together with other changing factors of political reality].
5. The transient nature and finiteness of prosperity of any form (whether among
forms of economic management or among forms of revolutionary movement) is
evidenced by the periodic renewal of crises (industrial, economic, financial,
political, social, etc.).
The reason for writing the January 1909 article "On the Road" [8, pp. 537–544]
was the organizational and ideo-political crisis in the Social-Democratic Party of
Russia. The background of the crisis lay in the urgent need to cleanse the
"workers' party of wavering, intellectual and petty-bourgeois elements who had
joined the labor movement mainly hoping for the imminent triumph of the
bourgeois-democratic revolution and who could not hold out during the reaction"
[8, p. 538]. The instability of these "elements" affected both theory, tactics and
organizational policy of the party. Conscious workers took charge of running
party organizations and leading them. The situation required convening the AllRussian Conference of the RSDLP, where answers were actually formulated
regarding what path the working-class party should choose in the difficult
current period.
The content of this answer consisted of the following decisions and developments
of the conference: "Marxist analysis of the current relationship between classes
and new policies of Tsarism"; indication of the immediate goal of struggle set by
the Social-Democratic Party; "assessment of lessons learned from the revolution
concerning the correctness of revolutionary-social democratic tactics; clarification
of causes of the party's crisis and pointing to the role of the proletarian element
of the party in combating it; resolving the issue of the ratio of illegal and legal
organization"; recognition of the need to use the Duma tribune and development
of precise guiding instructions for the social-democratic faction in connection with
direct criticism of its errors [8, p. 538].
Autocracy [instead of the term "autocracy", one can use today's equivalents
(terms closest and similar in meaning are): authoritarianism, autocracy, tyranny,
despotism] still acts as the main enemy of the proletariat and all democracy, but
it would be a mistake to think that it remains unchanged, does not change or
mimic. Today "autocracy attempts to take upon itself the solution of objectively
necessary tasks of the bourgeois revolution — creation of popular representation

 truly governing affairs of bourgeois society, and cleaning up medieval, tangled
and obsolete agrarian relations in the village; but precisely the practical result of
these new steps of autocracy turns out so far equal to zero, and this only makes
even clearer the necessity of other forces and means for solving the historical
task" [8, pp. 539–540].
New conditions of the moment require new forms of struggle: using the Duma
tribune appears an unconditional necessity; long-term work on education and
organization of masses of the proletariat is moved to the forefront; combining
illegal and legal organization presents special challenges to the party;
popularization and explanation of the experience of the revolution discredited by
liberals and liquidator intellectuals are needed both theoretically and practically.
But the tactical line of the party, which must manage to account for new
conditions in methods and tools of struggle, remains unchanged. The correctness
of revolutionary-social democratic tactics has been confirmed by the experience
of mass struggle of 1905–1907. The defeat of the revolution at the end of this
first campaign revealed not incorrectness of goals, not utopian nature of
objectives, not erroneousness of means and approaches, but insufficient
preparedness of forces, insufficient depth and breadth of the revolutionary crisis.
Let liberals and bewildered intelligentsia fall into despair after the first massive
battle for freedom. Conscious proletariat will respond to them that great tasks of
revolutions were solved only when advanced classes repeated their onslaught
more than once and achieved victory, having been taught by the experience of
defeats. Defeated armies learn well. Revolutionary classes of Russia have been
defeated in the first campaign, but the revolutionary situation persists. [Lenin's
inexhaustible optimism calling to learn also from defeats evokes nothing but
admiration!!!]. In new forms and another way, the revolutionary crisis looms
again, matures again [it is known that any crisis always precedes and ends with
replacement of forms representing developing contents of reality]. Long-term
preparation of broad masses — preparation taking into account higher and more
concrete goals — should be carried out, and the more successfully it is done, the
surer the victory in the new struggle will be. And the same proletariat will now
be able to patiently and steadfastly carry out the work of educating and
preparing new cadres of a mightier revolutionary force.
[It concerns periodic evaluation of the correlation of interacting components in
their relation and constant tracking of the trend of shifting this correlation
towards increasing and predominance of the more contentful component, for
which the contentfulness of the active component (i.e., the revolutionary spirit of
the proletariat) must be "replenished" through popularization and elucidation of
the experience of mass struggle and revolution].
Since the general link diluting and weakening Marxist ideology of the proletariat
continues to be the small commodity producer (petty bourgeoisie), drifting
between two clearly defined classes of capitalists and proletariat, then under
such circumstances the task of the day is: "Strengthening of the illegal party
organization, creating party cells in all areas of activity, creating above all purely
party, albeit few-membered workers' committees in every industrial enterprise,

 concentration of leading functions in the hands of leaders of the socialdemocratic movement from among the workers themselves" [8, p. 543].
Each cell and each party worker committee must become a support point for
agitational, propaganda and practically organizational work among the
masses, i.e., necessarily go where the mass goes and try at every step to push
its consciousness toward socialism, winning for itself leadership in all proletarian
legal organizations by virtue of its energy and ideological influence (rather than
titles and ranks).
[According to the testimony of N.V. Volsky (a contemporary of Vladimir
Ilyich, with the real surname N.V. Valentinov), who never was, by his own
admission, either a Bolshevik or a pronounced Menshevik [1], Lenin was a
supporter of the agitational work with all strata of the population, but the
emphasis proposed to be made nevertheless on the work with the proletariat
of Russia.]
In any case legally or semi-legally, openly or covertly, the working class will find
points of consolidation everywhere — conscious party social democrats will
always move ahead and consolidate among themselves to impact the masses in
the party spirit.
A party of the vanguard class (proletariat), which manages to organize its avantgarde and direct its forces so as to exert social-democratic influence on every
manifestation of life of the proletariat — this party will win no matter what [8, p.
544].
[By analogy with the previous article, V.I. Lenin bases his analysis of current
events again on the existence and interaction of two main classes: the ruling
class of owners of means of production and the subordinate class of nonpropertied, dependent hired laborers free from ownership of means of
production. Between these two classes drifts a layer of declassified pettybourgeois elements, periodically replenishing either class (much more often —
the class of non-propertied hired laborers). The cause of the ideological-political
crisis in the Russian Social-Democratic Party was exactly the uncertainty of
position of representatives of this stratum within the social-democratic milieu. All
other conclusions and fabrications stem from evil, belong to the realm of fictions
generated by apologists serving the ruling class among university professors,
professional philosophers, political scientists and propagandists of all stripes.
Neither Marx nor Lenin were discoverers of classes or originators of ideas about
class struggle as the driving force of social development — bourgeois historians
and economists had "exploited" these discoveries long before Marxism emerged.
But both used primarily these concepts and representations to analyze ongoing
historical processes, their patterns and trends.
Then came times when the aforementioned concepts (denoting the main
subjects of social activity and the process of its implementation) were buried

 under splinters and chips flying from the axe that carried out major public
transformations. Thus, the most important components of development and
their sacramental relations were put away in a drawer for a long time and
thoroughly forgotten.
Nowadays it is quite common to hold an opinion — usually expressed by the
same "court" politicians, economists and philosophers close to power
structures, as well as their media outlets justifying the fairness and eternity
of existing foundations, i.e., apologists of current social arrangements — that
class theory has hopelessly become obsolete and that now property
ownership itself (especially on means of production) plays no role;
supposedly, what matters today are opportunities to control financial flows.
No, gentlemen, you are wrong. In order to manage financial flows, play
multi-step financial combinations, rule over the whole world, etc., you still
have to eat, drink, live somewhere, "manage households, give birth to
children, produce products, exchange them..." (see the above-quoted Lenin
passage from the book “Materialism and Empiriocriticism”), which does not
allow ignoring property relations and everything connected with them. And if
you want to rise higher, soar above earthly life with its material physical side
— this will not happen either. To realize such a "wish", one would have to
completely detach oneself from the objectively-material level of one's bodilyintellectual organization, from the basis of your precious "I", which is
absolutely impossible without loss or deprivation of this unique "I". The level
of ideal subjective forms enters only narrowly (although being the
most contentful of reliably known ones today) into the overall set of levels
constituting your "I", whereas the bulk of every human "I" consists of rather
"down-to-earth" object-matter layers of reality. And you cannot get rid of the
heavy shackles of these "coarse" layers while remaining among those living
on earth. This is precisely what Marx called, recalling his words, the curse on
spirit — to be burdened by matter. And however much anyone might wish,
having achieved desired material prosperity, to dissociate themselves from
all coarse physicality and ascend to the realm of the ideal and unearthly —
property relations and especially those regarding means of production will
continue to remain key, whoever says otherwise and however they try to
camouflage this fact. Therefore, staying on real ground and being part of the
object-matter level of reality forming and filling you up, you will inevitably
have to keep fighting for your flesh and for your place under the sun. You will
also inevitably have to think about your offspring, and in connection with this
— about inheritance for your descendants, i.e., about that very mundane
property which, god forbid, may end up in alien hands. Your own flesh will
not let you soar above the struggle and beyond this entire world like an elf or
angel; but once you shed it (if such should ever occur), you will
simultaneously lose yourself (your "I") together with all your "fantasies" and
"desires" — well, then what will your desires concern?
The direct path for you, gentlemen, lies toward socialism — there alone will
you find deliverance from unbearable fetters of property and endless

 thoughts about accumulation and transfer of material inheritance into the
right hands, and finally begin caring about intellectual and spiritual legacy;
there you will acquire more or less genuine freedom from dreary thoughts
about how to master financial assets, ride financial flows — and who knows
what else you cling to with iron grip. Welcome to socialism, gentlemen!
It must be said that denial of classes and class struggle is an inexhaustible
element of idle reasoning exercises, periodically reviving and again taking
possession of unsophisticated minds after each successive "defeat" and
public expulsion. It seems, however, that the hour has come when public
attention is drawn again to relations of key constituents of developing reality,
as well as to their role and significance during replacement of forms of social
progress. The mere absence at present of visible signs of class struggle
speaks only of disorganization or insufficient organization of representatives
of hired labor and lack of outstanding and incorruptible leaders of
revolutionary movement at this stage of social development.]
In relation {proletariat/autocracy (tsarism)} a fairly noticeable shift occurred
towards predominance of the fastest-developing contentful component —
proletariat with its Marxist party, becoming richer in content due to growth in
educational standard of party and proletarian ranks, while the second
component — autocracy — mimics, tries to mask itself as bourgeoisie and
merge with it. It should be noted that in his analysis Lenin never considers
the main interacting components or figures separately, detached from each
other — always only together, in interaction, in relation. Proletariat is
nonessential without bourgeoisie or capitalists, just as the latter are
nonessential without proletariat. Capital is nonessential without hired labor,
and vice versa. Only the interaction of these two constituents of reality, their
collision, their conflict, internecine struggle contributes to emergence of new
developmental forms and movement toward a new socio-economic
formation, i.e., to new forms of acquiring social orders.
[Periodically arising public conflicts have as their foundation accumulating
unsolvable-for-the-time-being content-form contradictions:
between
outdated management system, bureaucratized power, "bourgeoisified" ruling
class with its institutions and forms of governance on the one hand, and, on
the other hand, competence and preparedness of society with its substantive
public opinions and representations surpassing this "ossifying" system.
Evidence of this includes numerous examples of modern states with their
internal conflicts: frames, forms, methods of primitive management do not
meet the needs, demands, requirements of a complexifying, perfecting,
developing and rapidly increasing-in-contentfulness socium.]
A crisis in the revolutionary movement (according to Lenin) is a harbinger of
another stage of construction and formation of a new relation of directly
interacting constituents-components and at the same time a precursor of a
new search for a way "on the road" and purification from the old form (its
attributes) restraining the movement of the contentful constituent; it is a

 sign of outgrowing the existing form by its developed content and an
indicator of necessity to master a new promising form sufficiently developed
already in terms of content. At the same time, the correlation of
constituents-components in the newly emerging and changing relation is
analyzed, where the numerator is enriched by decisions and conclusions of
conferences and congresses of the Bolshevik Party, while the denominator is
fed by resolutions of the Constituent Assembly of the State Duma (i.e.,
circulars of the "mimicking" form of state government).
[Production, management, economic, ideological-political, etc., crises are
indicators of a disrupted balance or equilibrium between interacting components
in their various form-relations. The leading contentful constituent moving
forward (or preparing to move forward and lead) "requires" search for and
discovery of its corresponding formal component that balances (for some period
of time) the combined relation of these constituents. The stagnant phase in
which this new disequilibrium relation finds itself (in our case: {educated
proletariat/mimicking autocracy}) is overcome by searching for and finding a
more active form of movement of the contentful component, which, when
another way out "on the road" is found, is ensured through accelerated increase
in contentfulness of the numerator of the mentioned new relation; i.e., through
(in Lenin's words): indication of the immediate goal of struggle; assessment of
correctness of social-democratic tactics; clarification of causes of the party crisis
and pointing to the role of the proletarian element of the party in combating it;
resolution of the issue regarding the ratio of illegal and legal organization;
recognition of the need to use the Duma tribune and development of precise
guiding instructions for the social-democratic faction.]
And, as Lenin summarizes, this stage must be outgrown and the crisis overcome
by discovering and applying new forms of struggle [8, p. 540].
In other words, a new exit "on the road" is sought through increasing
the contentfulness of forms of the Social-Democratic movement.
§ 2. Works of the immediate pre-revolutionary period
The second period, which we have named as immediate pre-revolutionary
(on the eve of the revolution), is represented by a number of works by
Vladimir I. Lenin, dictated by rapidly changing events (especially on the eve
of the October coup).
1. In the book "On the Right of Nations to Self-Determination" [8, pp.
569-621], written in May 1914, Lenin analyzes in detail the specifics of
applying the Marxist position on the secession of nations depending on
different historically established conditions for the formation of one or
another nation.
Due to its closest connection with the present, we will dwell on this work in
more detail.

 Preliminarily, it should be said that the "right of nations to selfdetermination", regarding the legitimacy and expediency of whose
proclamation and protection heated debates do not cease even in our days, is
not a figment of V.I. Lenin's imagination or an invention of the Bolsheviks,
but the result of discussions and decisions of the International congresses,
and in particular the "London International Congress (of socialist workers'
parties and trade unions) of 1896". The defense of this right and its inclusion
in the program of the Social-Democratic Party of Russia was justified by
Lenin by referring to the corresponding stage of the national liberation
movement experienced by Russia. By analogy with the support by Marxists
under similar historical conditions of the said right in Western Europe, Lenin,
focusing on similar liberation processes in Eastern Europe and Asia (including
Russia), but occurring with some delay (at least by half a century), concludes
on the necessity of advancing the same demand at the stage of revolutionary
transformations in Russia as well.
To convey the logic of Lenin's thought, let us provide a chain of characteristic
quotes from this work.
"An unconditional requirement of Marxist theory in the analysis of any social
question whatsoever is to place it within definite historical limits, and then, if
the question concerns one country (for example, a national program for a
given country), to take into account the concrete specifics distinguishing this
country from others within the limits of one and the same historical epoch"
[8, p. 574].
"The comparison of the political and economic development of different
countries, as well as their Marxist programs, is of enormous significance from
the standpoint of Marxism, for both the general capitalist nature of modern
states and the general law of their development are indisputable. But such a
comparison must be made skillfully. The ABC condition here is to clarify
the question of whether the historical epochs of development of the
compared countries are comparable" [8, p. 578].
"In Western, continental Europe, the era of bourgeois-democratic revolutions
covers a rather definite time span, approximately from 1789 to 1871. It was
precisely this era that was the era of national movements and the creation of
national states. Upon the completion of this era, Western Europe turned into
an established system of bourgeois states, as a general rule, at the same
time nationally unified states. Therefore, to now seek the right to selfdetermination in the programs of West European socialists means not to
understand the ABC of Marxism.
In Eastern Europe and Asia, the era of bourgeois-democratic revolutions only
began in 1905. ...And in this chain of events only a blind man can fail to see
the awakening of a whole series of bourgeois-democratic national
movements, aspirations for the creation of nationally independent and

 nationally unified states. It is precisely because and only because
Russia, together with neighboring countries, is experiencing this era
that we need a point on the right of nations to self-determination in
our program" [8, pp. 578-579].
"Thus, it is the historical concrete specifics of the national question in
Russia that give us a special urgency to the recognition of the right
of nations to self-determination in the epoch we are experiencing" [8,
p. 581].
"The bourgeoisie, which naturally acts as the hegemon (leader) of any
national movement at its beginning, calls the support of all national
aspirations a practical matter. But the policy of the proletariat in the national
question (as in other questions) only supports the bourgeoisie in a certain
direction, but never coincides with its policy. ...Every bourgeoisie wants in
national matters either privileges for its nation or exclusive benefits for it;
this is called 'practical'. The proletariat is against any privileges, against
any exclusivity" [8, p. 582].
"The bourgeoisie always places its national demands in the foreground. It
puts them unconditionally. For the proletariat, they are subordinated to the
interests of the class struggle. Theoretically, one cannot guarantee in
advance whether the secession of a given nation or its equal status with
another nation will complete the bourgeois-democratic revolution; for the
proletariat, it is important in both cases to ensure the development of its
class; for the bourgeoisie, it is important to hinder this development,
postponing its tasks before the tasks of 'their' nation. Therefore, the
proletariat limits itself to a negative, so to speak, demand for the recognition
of the right to self-determination, guaranteeing nothing to any nation,
undertaking to give nothing regarding another nation.
Let this be not 'practical', but in fact this most reliably guarantees the most
democratic of possible solutions; the proletariat needs only these guarantees,
and the bourgeoisie of each nation needs guarantees of its benefits without
relation to the position (to possible minuses) of other nations.
The bourgeoisie is most interested in the 'feasibility' of a given demand —
hence the eternal policy of deals with the bourgeoisie of other
nations to the detriment of the proletariat.
Let this be not 'practical' for opportunists, but this is the only guarantee in
fact, a guarantee of maximum national equality and peace in spite of both
the feudal lords and the nationalist bourgeoisie.
The entire task of the proletarians in the national question is
'impractical' from the standpoint of the nationalist bourgeoisie of
each nation, for the proletarians demand abstract equality, the
principled absence of the slightest privileges, being hostile to any
nationalism.

 ...The proletariat is against such practicality: recognizing equality and equal
right to a national state, it values and places above all the union of
proletarians of all nations, evaluating any national demand, any national
secession from the angle of the class struggle of workers. The slogan of
practicality is in fact merely the slogan of uncritical adoption of bourgeois
aspirations.
They tell us: by supporting the right to secession, you support bourgeois
nationalism of oppressed nations. ...We answer: no, it is precisely the
bourgeoisie that is interested in a 'practical' solution here, while for the
workers it is important to fundamentally distinguish two tendencies. Since
the bourgeoisie of the oppressed nation is fighting the oppressing one, we
are always and in any case and more resolutely than all, for we are the
boldest and most consistent enemies of oppression. Since the bourgeoisie of
the oppressed nation stands for its bourgeois nationalism, we are against.
The struggle against the privileges and violence of the oppressing
nation and no connivance at the striving for privileges on the part of
the oppressed nation.
If we do not advance and conduct in our agitation the slogan of the right to
secession, we will play into the hands not only of the bourgeoisie, but also of
the feudal lords and the absolutism of the oppressing nation. ...In every
bourgeois nationalism of an oppressed nation there is a general-democratic
content against oppression, and it is this content that we unconditionally
support, strictly separating the striving for one's own national exclusiveness,
fighting against the striving of the Polish bourgeois to oppress the Jew, etc.,
etc. [That is, here, undoubtedly, one must see the boundary markers beyond
which the striving for national identity degenerates into inveterate
nationalism and then into bestial Nazism, and suppress such a content-form
transformation].
This is "impractical" from the point of view of the bourgeois and the
philistine. This is the only practical and principled and truly helping
democracy, freedom, and the proletarian union policy in the national
question: recognition of the right of nations to secession for all; evaluation of
each specific question of secession from the standpoint eliminating any
inequality, any privileges, any exclusivity.
Let us take the position of the oppressing nation. Can a people that
oppresses other peoples be free? No. The interests of freedom of the
Great Russian population require a struggle against such oppression.
A long history, a centuries-old history of suppressing the movements
of oppressed nations, systematic propaganda of such suppression by
the "higher" classes have created enormous obstacles to the cause of
freedom of the Great Russian people itself in its prejudices, etc.

 ...The Great Russian proletariat cannot achieve its goals, cannot clear
its path to freedom, without systematically fighting these prejudices.
[And the matter here, perhaps, is not only in prejudices or the moralhumanistic side of the issue, but also in the trivial discomfort of the everyday
life of the oppressing nation, being in constant tension, suspicion,
apprehensions and expectation of blows in the back from the oppressed,
suppressed, humiliated nation.
The Great Russian, privileged in relation to a non-Russian, is just as unfree,
uneasy, unbalanced, unself-sufficient as a non-Russian — due to the social
tension created by the counter-resistance and opposition from the oppressed
nation. This contentfulness ought to be known to today's "resolvers" of the
national question].
...We, the proletarians, declare ourselves in advance to be opponents of
Great Russian privileges and in this direction conduct all our propaganda and

Let this propaganda be impractical from the point of view of the

"To accuse the supporters of the freedom of self-determination, i.e. the
freedom of secession, of encouraging separatism is the same stupidity and

"The real class significance of the liberal hostility to the principle of political

 ...The interests of the working class and its struggle against capitalism
require full solidarity and the closest unity of workers of all nations, require

Therefore, a deviation from the tasks of proletarian policy and the
subordination of workers to bourgeois policy would be both if the SocialDemocrats were to deny the right to self-determination, i.e. the right to
secession of oppressed nations, and if the Social-Democrats were to support
all national demands of the bourgeoisie of oppressed nations. To a hired
worker it is all the same whether his predominant exploiter will be the Great
Russian bourgeoisie preferably over a non-Russian one, or the Polish
preferably over a Jewish one, etc. A hired worker who has realized the
interests of his class is indifferent both to the state privileges of the
Great Russian capitalists and to the promises of the Polish or
Ukrainian capitalists that paradise on earth will be established when
they possess state privileges.
...In any case, the hired worker will remain an object of exploitation, and a
successful struggle against it requires the independence of the proletariat
from nationalism, the complete, so to speak, neutrality of the proletarians in
the struggle of the bourgeoisie of different nations for supremacy. The
slightest support by the proletariat of any nation for the privileges of "its"
national bourgeoisie will inevitably cause distrust of the proletariat of another
nation, will weaken the international class solidarity of workers, will divide
them to the delight of the bourgeoisie. And the denial of the right to selfdetermination, or to secession, inevitably means in practice support for the
privileges of the dominant nation" [8, pp. 594-595].
"In the question of the self-determination of nations, as in any other
question, we are interested first of all in the self-determination of the
proletariat within nations" [8, p. 597].
[Nowadays, such an approach remains topical, counting on the unification of
all wage workers (regardless of nations and nationality) in the struggle and
opposition to the associated oligarchy.
In the application to the present day, everywhere in the text of Lenin's work,
by the proletariat one should understand the wage workers and
representatives of wage labor, and by the bourgeoisie of the oppressing and
oppressed nation — the foreign and local oligarchy. After making such a

before the October Revolution. We are obviously being punished today
for Unlearned lessons of dialectics, as negligent students, although
we have already passed all this once.
To please their personal interests (i.e., in pursuit of profit), the bourgeoisie
(oligarchy) of any nation easily steps over national and patriotic principles,

 which fully justifies the label "comprador" (venal) bourgeoisie hung on it.
This, first of all, must be known and kept in mind by every people trying to
find the roots of national troubles. Only a consciously organized opposition
to the market (i.e., spontaneously) "molded" oligarchy can change the
position (and status) of the working people for the better. Today's
bourgeoisie, like the bourgeoisie of the past, are also not interested in social
development (i.e., in improving methods of management and planning,
economic and political reforms, raising the standard of living of the
population), since all this contributes to the growth of consciousness,
education and, accordingly, organization of wage workers. Therefore, no
one is in a hurry, and will not be, to transfer or invest their foreign savings
and capital (allegedly earned "by their own sweat and blood") into the
country's economy, to abandon offshore assets.
What allows us to confidently use in this connection the terms "oligarchs",
"oligarchy"? It is enough to look more closely at the structure of property,
income and acquisitions of any major official or deputy (not losing sight of
relatives and trusted persons with assets rewritten to them) to see there

profitable industrial enterprises and banks, and owners of large property,
owners of bank accounts and financial assets, and, moreover, undoubtedly,
those residing in power. And then how do such managers differ from

analysis, all the so-called oligarchs differ from each other only in the size of
