into account — otherwise, in the absence of means of suppression, social
inequality or imbalance could not be maintained for an indefinitely long

 time). The arming of the bourgeoisie against the proletariat is one of the most
basic facts of capitalist society. And to proclaim the slogan of disarmament for
the proletariat against this background is tantamount to abandoning the point of
view of the class struggle. On the contrary, the arming of the proletariat is the
only possible tactic of the revolutionary class, a tactic dictated by the entire
objective development of capitalist militarism, prescribed by this development.
And therefore our slogan should be the arming of the proletariat [i.e. increasing
the contentfulness of the form (the proletarian class) at a certain — force — sublevel of this form] in order to defeat and disarm the bourgeoisie. Saying that
"capitalist society was and always is horror without end", Lenin masterfully notes
the trend of piling up contentful accumulations conditioned by military actions,
leading to "an end with horror" (a terrible end). And at the same time, contrary
to established beliefs, behind this "terrible end" he sees the emergence and
emergence of a new form and, accordingly, a new perspective, consisting in the
fact that "before everyone's eyes, by the forces of the bourgeoisie itself, the only
legitimate and revolutionary war is being prepared, namely: civil war against the
imperialist bourgeoisie" [8, p. 755] with a new contentful turn in the course of
the upcoming contentful transformations and transformations.
"Now militarization penetrates all public life" [8, p. 756]: today the imperialist
bourgeoisie militarizes the entire male population, including youth, and in the
plans for tomorrow — the militarization of women as well. Regarding this, one
can say: so much the better, the sooner and closer to the armed uprising against
capitalism. Mastering military science is necessary for the proletariat not in order
to shoot at their brothers, workers of other countries, as is done in the current
war, but in order to fight against the bourgeoisie of their own country, to put an
end to exploitation, poverty and wars not by kind wishes and hopes, by
statements of condemnation and concern, but by victory over the bourgeoisie
and disarming it, which is achieved only by waging war against war, i.e. by civil
confrontation and civil war.
The main disadvantage of the demand for disarmament lies precisely in the fact
that all concrete questions of the revolution are left unattended (ignored). The
"disarmament" of the proletariat (people), Lenin insists, professed by conciliators
with the bourgeoisie of all stripes (opportunists, following Lenin's terminology), is
precisely an escape from the vile reality, and not a struggle against it [the
fundamental transformation of the established reality is possible only by decisive
actions with weapons in hand]. The struggle against imperialism, not connected
with the struggle against opportunism, is an empty phrase and a deception. The
main danger emanating from all varieties of opportunism [i.e. conciliation and
apostasy] is that they hush up (or talk out) the question of the connection of the
ongoing war with the revolution and thus come out with a new absurd slogan:
revolution without weapons [8, pp. 757-758].
Furthermore, the bourgeoisie of all great imperialist powers has become so
reactionary [i.e. striving to avoid crisis and restore the lost balance in affairs]
and so imbued with the striving for world domination [i.e. to achieve
their contentful superiority] that any war on the part of the bourgeoisie of these

 countries can only be reactionary. The proletariat should be not only against any
such war, but should wish for the defeat of "its" government in such wars and
use it for a revolutionary armed uprising, if an uprising with the aim of
preventing the war fails [8, pp. 758-759].
With the conciliators (fighters for the disarmament of the people) one cannot
fight by means of programs alone, but only by means of relentless observation
to ensure that they are actually implemented. The largest fatal mistake of the
bankrupt Second International was that the word did not correspond to the
deed, that a habit of hypocrisy and shameless revolutionary phrase was
cultivated. Disarmament as a social idea is generated, obviously, by the special
"peaceful" living conditions of individual small states, which have stood aside
from the bloody world road of wars for quite a long time and hope to remain so.
The petty-bourgeois desire to stay away from the great battles of world history,
to use their relatively monopolistic position for passivity — this is the objective
social environment that can provide the idea of disarmament with a certain
success and a certain spread in some small states. Of course, this aspiration is
reactionary and rests on illusions, for imperialism one way or another drags
small states into the whirlpool of the world economy and world politics. [This
"wonderful" side or feature of the arrangement of "well-fed" lazy, arrogantly
haughty communities and societies must always be taken into account: their
impudently-pushy essence can be overcome by active persistent impact on them
until the moment of their scattering to their shelters; brave and "pushy" at first,
they are not able to withstand a long siege and continuous onslaught, leading to
their physiological discomfort or threatening complete physical destruction].
Switzerland, for example, its imperialist situation prescribes two lines of the
workers' movement: 1) the opportunists in alliance with the bourgeoisie strive to
turn Switzerland into a republican-democratic monopolistic union to profit from
the tourists of the imperialist bourgeoisie and so that this "peaceful" monopolistic
position (a quiet "harbor") is as profitable as possible [here lie the roots of the
success, prosperity and well-being of neutral dwarf states like Switzerland and
the like. The quiet "backwaters" of Switzerland and similar small lands, where
one can sit out and hide one's savings in days of great crises and upheavals,
were prepared by the rich for themselves in advance — that is why these "areas"
received such a lush bloom in inviolability]; 2) the real Social-Democrats of
Switzerland seek to use the relative freedom and "international" position of
Switzerland to help the close alliance of revolutionary elements of the workers'
parties of Europe to win.
[Both lines are conditioned by the special position and the historically established
status quo of a small country].
Proceeding from these two pronounced tendencies, it becomes clear, Lenin sums
up, that objectively "disarmament" is a specifically national program of small
states, and by no means an international program of revolutionary international
Social-Democracy [8, pp. 759-761].

 And then the hottest pre-revolutionary times came. One would think that the
rhetoric and style of Lenin's articles should have become chaotic and less
ordered; however, no — all the same sustained and balanced tone, the same
unhurried, patient deep analysis, the unhurried course of the presentation of
thought, which lead to the most correct remarkable conclusions, based by no
means on unfounded calls and slogans, but on the ability to see the general
objective behind individual specific facts, i.e. to guess and expose the regular
in the process of building a dialectically verified scheme of analysis.
6. Small in volume, but extremely rich in Content and permeated through and
through with the spirit of dialectics, the article "On Dual Power" [9, pp. 16-18]
was written in April 1917. The fundamental question of any revolution, Lenin
writes at the beginning of the article, is the question of power in the state. But
the remarkable peculiarity of the current revolution is that it has created dual
power, which no one thought of or could think of before. Therefore, the old
"formulas" of Bolshevism must be supplemented and corrected. Dual power
consists in the fact that next to the Provisional Government of the bourgeoisie,
another government has emerged: the Soviets of Workers' and Soldiers'
Deputies. Thus, there is a relation composed or formed of two sidescomponents: {"growing" government of the people in the face of the Soviets of
Workers' and Soldiers' (i.e. peasants dressed in soldiers' uniforms) Deputies /
government of the bourgeoisie}. The peculiarity of the people's power consists in
the fact that it: firstly, represents a revolutionary dictatorship, since its source is
not the law, but the direct initiative of the masses from below, i.e.
revolutionary
"seizure"
[the
source
of
power
is
some
internal contentful (energetic) constituent of reality, determining the deep
striving of the people (or a group of people); power itself is the external form of
acquiring this contentful constituent]; secondly, it carries out the replacement of
the police and the army by the armed people; thirdly, it places officials and the
bureaucracy under the control of the armed people with the possibility of
replacing personnel at the first demand of the people and paying labor no higher
than the usual wage of a good worker [this extremely important and remarkable
move (technique) of the nascent power was invented by no means by Lenin and
the Bolsheviks, but was only successfully and justifiably implemented by the
Bolshevik government after the victory of the Great October Socialist Revolution.
This was an act approved by the people, in confirmation of the establishment of
a more just distribution of the worked-out product. By the way, both the
"Soviets" and our proud word "comrade" and many other similar fashionable
terms and concepts of that time are also not inventions of Lenin and company,
but verbal constructions corresponding to the achievements of the advanced
enlightened thought of that time, skillfully used by the Bolsheviks in organizing
the public arrangement of a new type]. Thus, a state is formed according to the
type of the Paris Commune of 1871.
At the same time, this is only an embryonic power, for it still yields positions to
the bourgeoisie. The reason is the insufficient consciousness and organization of
the proletarians and peasants. The uncertainty of the new power is revealed by
the simple question it poses: should the Provisional Government be overthrown

 immediately? Lenin answers this question as follows: 1) the government must
be overthrown — for it is oligarchic, bourgeois, and not nationwide, it can give
neither peace, nor bread, nor freedom; 2) however, it cannot be overthrown
now, for it is held together by a formal and actual agreement with the Soviets of
Workers' Deputies; 3) it cannot be overthrown in the usual way at all, for it relies
on the support of the bourgeoisie by the Council of Workers' Deputies, which is
the only possible revolutionary government, directly expressing the
consciousness and will of the majority of workers and peasants (and above,
better than this type of government, as the Soviets of workers, farm laborers,
peasant, soldier deputies, humanity has not developed and we still do not know).
Hence, "to become power, conscious workers must win the majority over to their
side: as long as there is no violence against the masses, there is no
other way to power" [9, p. 18].
The bourgeoisie is for the sole power of the bourgeoisie, while the conscious
workers are for the sole power of the Soviets of workers, farm laborers, peasant
and soldier deputies, for sole power prepared by the clarification of proletarian
consciousness and its liberation from the influence of the bourgeoisie, and not by
adventures [i.e. the current relation from the indicated components (see above)
must now be enriched with content, saturated with contentfulness by feeding its
upper component, the "numerator", with Content, in order to strengthen it as
the leading component by clarifying and enriching the proletarian
consciousness].
Thus, as we see, again guided by the dialectical method, Lenin precisely and
unambiguously determines both the relation of the main componentsconstituents of development at this particular stage of the revolutionary
movement, and the actual class correlation of forces-components within the
relation composed by him, which determines (we are talking about the
correlation) the tasks for the near-term development of the revolutionary
situation and the direction of the subsequent movement or change of this
relation as a whole.
[This article is a classic example of skillful, filigree mastery of dialectics and its
effective application].
7. In the article "Three Crises" [9, pp. 124-127], written by Lenin in July 1917,
various forms of the course of the revolution are considered (primarily from class
positions). Three objective political crises that determined the nature of the
course of the revolutionary process of that period served as the basis for lies and
slander [i.e. numerous "fakes", as they would say in our time] about the artificial
organization of these crises by the hands of the Bolsheviks. Objectively common
to all three crises is the "overflowing" discontent of the people with the
bourgeoisie and its government, which allows us to see behind all this the
incessant class struggle. Individually in these crises — these are different forms
of conducting (manifestation) of the mentioned class struggle. In all three cases
— this is a demonstration, but: in the first case — stormy-spontaneous,
unorganized, leading to shooting at the demonstrators by the Black Hundreds; in

 the second case — appointed by the Bolsheviks, canceled and postponed to a
new date, a general more powerful demonstration with the predominance of
Bolshevik slogans; in the third case — a spontaneous rise of counter-revolution
contrary to the efforts of the Bolsheviks.
An instructive conclusion from the events under consideration, as Lenin notes, is
"that all three crises show us a certain. new in the history of our revolution, form
of a demonstration of a more complex type, with a wave-like movement [from
extreme to extreme], a rapid rise and a steep fall, with an aggravation of the
revolution and counter-revolution, with the "washing out", for a more or less
long time, of the middle elements" [9, pp. 125-126].
Lenin masterfully notes that in such periods of acute political crises, the
contradictions between the main "players" of the revolutionary action are
aggravated [in this case between the components of the very main relation
{proletariat/bourgeoisie}], while some intermediate "middle elements"
accompanying every turmoil are pushed aside: "But the point is that this is not
an ordinary demonstration, it is much more than a demonstration and less than
a revolution. This is an explosion of revolution and counter-revolution together,
this is a sharp, sometimes almost sudden "washing out" of the middle elements
in connection with the stormy manifestation of proletarian and bourgeois
[elements]" [9, p. 126].
The objective clash of two opposing sides, two classes — the proletariat and the
bourgeoisie — corresponds to the political struggle of their parties — the
Bolsheviks and the Cadets. At the same time, the "middle elements" accuse the
Cadets that they facilitate the work of the Bolsheviks, and the Bolsheviks that
they facilitate the work of the Cadets. Now, Lenin says, if instead of political
names we substitute class ones, then we get the dreams of the petty bourgeoisie
about the "disappearance" of the class struggle between the proletariat and the
bourgeoisie. And then follows an objective and dialectically verified conclusion
that no Bolsheviks in the world could have "caused" not only three, but even one
"popular movement", if the deepest economic and political reasons did not
set the proletariat in motion, that no Cadets and monarchists together can
cause any movement "from the right", if equally deep reasons did not create
the counter-revolutionary nature of the bourgeoisie as a class [9, pp.
126-127].
This is an indicator of the petty bourgeoisie's misunderstanding of the
mechanism or essence of the class struggle of the proletariat against the
bourgeoisie. Since the vast majority of the country's population is pettybourgeois in their life situation and even more so in their ideas, and in the
confrontation with large capital (in the face of banks and syndicates in the first
place) the urban proletariat is not yet capable of immediately winning over the
majority of the semi-proletarians and other strata of the population, such an
objectively formed situation [corresponding to the objectively formed at the
current moment correlation of force-components in the main class relation

 {proletariat/bourgeoisie}] will be expressed in the inevitability of crises similar to
the three crises under consideration in their three forms.
[Economic and political crises (the confrontation of two deeply non-equilibrium
components of the known relation {proletariat/bourgeoisie}) set in motion both
the revolutionary proletariat (with its form of government or power — the
Soviets of workers', soldiers' and peasants' deputies) on the one hand, and the
counter-revolutionary bourgeoisie (with its form of government — the Provisional
Government) on the other. At the same time, the "middle elements" (petty
bourgeoisie) with their parties (the Socialist-Revolutionaries and the Mensheviks)
lash both of them for "rocking" the common boat. Behind the forms of the
erupting crises, Lenin clearly sees their essence — the interaction, struggle,
conflict of two components of development, two main sides of the relation
{proletariat/bourgeoisie}. The middle elements or petty bourgeoisie (including
the intelligentsia) are always an oscillating stratum, which, depending on the
circumstances, can play the role of both a revolutionary-active and a counterrevolutionary element. And such oscillations from one pole to the other are
inevitable, which leads to both a change in the established correlation between
the sides and a change in the relation itself as a whole.
That is why, in the final analysis, for the implementation of a full-fledged
uprising, the proletariat today lacks a "critical mass" and therefore the topical
(for now) task is to win over the oscillating semi-proletarian mass to its
proletarian side, including the poorest peasantry and the petty-bourgeois
stratum of the country's population. In this case, we are talking about the need
to increase the contentfulness of the "upper" component (the "numerator" of the
given relation, i.e. the consciousness and organization of the proletariat) in the
actually formed relation of components {proletariat/bourgeoisie} by all possible
means, including explanatory work, agitation, and propaganda.]
8. Lenin's attitude to his probable arrest in the hot July days of 1917 will be
shown by the example of the publications of two of his small articles "Where is
the Power and Where is the Counter-Revolution" [9, pp. 119-123] and "On
the Question of the Appearance in Court of the Bolshevik Leaders" [9,
pp. 128-129].
In the first article, the false statement of a certain former member of the State
Duma about the readiness of Lenin and the Bolshevik party to conclude a
separate peace with Germany is analyzed, despite the fact that Lenin, on the
contrary, has always and unconditionally rejected a separate peace with
Germany in the most resolute and irrevocable manner [9, p. 121]. This same
source reported that the Bolshevik leaders received money from German agents.
At the same time, everyone perfectly understood that if this information were
true, the General Staff would by no means allow its premature leakage to the
yellow press and would not hesitate for a minute to arrest the Bolshevik top.
In fact, as it turned out later, taking advantage of dual power (or rather, the
powerlessness of that period), this information for the purpose of discrediting the

 Bolsheviks was spread by the so-called behind-the-scenes counter-revolution —
the Cadets, well-known circles of the General Staff and the Black Hundred press.
"The counter-revolution takes advantage of the powerlessness, uniting the
Cadets with the well-known commanding tops of the army and with the Black
Hundred press" [9, p. 123].
The second article on the question of the appearance of the Bolshevik leaders in
court brings on this account, as one would expect, two opinions: to appear and
not to appear. At first, Lenin very seriously considered the possibility of his
presence in court, since such a step would allow using the court as a tribune to
clarify the essence of the Bolsheviks' position and additional agitation, to which
Ilyich always approached very scrupulously. Moreover, Lenin was by no means a
man of a timid disposition to be frightened by threats from the Provisional
Government. However, after a comprehensive collective discussion of this
option, the VI Congress of the RSDLP(b) unanimously adopted a resolution in
which it spoke out against the appearance of Lenin and a number of other
comrades in court, foreseeing a possible massacre of the Bolshevik leadership
[or, as they would say today, the neutralization of the entire party asset].
"If we assume that in Russia there is and a correct government is possible, a
correct court, the convening of the Constituent Assembly is probable, then one
can come to a conclusion in favor of appearance" [9, p. 128]. However, due to
the absence of power [the established dual power as an equivalent to
powerlessness], there was neither a correct court, nor a correct government, nor
a Constituent Assembly in Russia at that time. The court is supposedly fair, the
court will figure it out, the court will be public, the people will understand — "a
reasoning naive to childishness". It is not a court, but a persecution of
internationalists, that is what Kerensky and Co. needed. Therefore, "let the
internationalists work illegally as much as they can, but let them not make the
stupidity of voluntary appearance!" [9, p. 129].
[How honestly, responsibly and devotedly Lenin treated his cause, involving the
implementation of the socialist idea in life, how convinced he was of the
rightness of this idea, can be judged by the memoirs of his contemporaries, even
from among those who were not Bolsheviks and never shared their views. The
Menshevik F. Dan, for example, once remarked with irritation: "...There is no
longer such a person who would be busy with the revolution 24 hours a day,
who would have no other thoughts except the thought of the revolution, and
who even sees only the revolution in his dreams. Just try to cope with such a
one" [13, p. 6].
Can Lenin's devotion to the common cause, his lack of greed and purposefulness
be compared with the qualities of today's "rulers" or the so-called Duma
communists and all other "zealots for the people" — with their camouflaged
financial assets, unaffordable real estate and "treacherously" tinted bank
accounts (including foreign ones). It's laughable, really. Can the current "rulers"
and their ilk compare with Lenin's pleiad of state leaders, who descended into

 the grave in the same frock coats in which they came into the revolutionary
political movement, and then into power?
Every "ruler" has, by and large, only two options for "exit" from power structures
when the earth is shaking underfoot and power is slipping from his hands. The
first option: to inconspicuously "merge", saving one's "hide" (in modern
language), changing into a woman's dress or (which is tantamount to the same
thing) timely pulling a retirement pajamas on oneself; the second option: again,
saving one's precious hide, to apply force against the rebels.
Because his own "priceless" life and excessive ambitions are at stake, the
modern "ruler" readily and without hesitation is ready to deploy against his own
people artillery, tanks, MLRS and aircraft, perfectly realizing that all this is a
weapon of group destruction. And how should one treat such a nonentity after
that?
And against such a background, someone has the tongue to make claims to
Lenin, who was not smeared and not noticed in anything similar (i.e., never
clung to power and did not allow anything of the kind and close, which cannot be
said about many other characters — once former and now residing in power). In
this regard, Lenin was always guided by the principle formulated in one of his
reports: "A revolution is worth something only if it knows how to defend itself...".
It was about defense and the struggle against counter-revolution, which in every
way and by all methods, including terror, sought to prevent the formation of a
new social order (new socio-economic formation) and the creative
transformation of the country: "The revolution was an awakening to a new life of
millions. In February and March, these millions did not know what they were
going to continue the slaughter into which they were driven by the tsars and
Kerenskys and the purpose of which was exposed only in December by the
Bolshevik government. This turning point has come; it changes the strength of
the revolution. If these masses have now created a new discipline in the Red
Army, not the discipline of the stick and the landlord's, but the discipline of the
Soviets of workers' and peasants' deputies; if they are now going to the greatest
self-sacrifice; if among them a new cohesion has developed, it is because for the
first time in the consciousness and experience of tens of millions a new, socialist
discipline is being born and has been born, the Red Army has been born. It was
born only when these tens of millions of people saw from their own experience
that they themselves had overthrown the landlords and capitalists, that a new
life was being built, that they themselves had begun to build it and that they
would build this life if a foreign invasion did not interfere" [12, pp. 122-123].
For the current "rulers", for example, special cycles of television programs are
organized so that they explain their most "humane" and "sweet-tempered"
impulses, talk about their grandiose plans, diligently winding flour products of
well-known names onto the ear shells of undiscriminating or confused listeners.
And as a result or in the dry residue, there will still be the same two options for
"exit" from "power": either quietly "merge" in women's underwear or retirement
pajamas, so that no one can "catch" the poor fellow for the miscalculations made

 in foreign and domestic policy, or drown everything in human blood for the sake
of one's own salvation. And there should be no illusions about this. Wretches of
all stripes who have got into power use all possible means to stay afloat or get
out dry.
Meanwhile, every such "ruler" should see at the end of his term of office not a
comfortable armchair with a woolen blanket, but a block with an axe; only then
can one hope that he will check every step he takes and make every decision in
the name of and for the benefit of the people, who have temporarily delegated
their power powers to him].
To our great regret, many modern "rulers" (including Russian ones) still, as
in the past, build up for themselves, cherish and nurture oligarchicplutocratic states: a) according to their perverted ideas of the ideal (in the
sense of perfect) world order; b) as a natural product and indicator of their
lack of education and bad taste. Moreover, to develop or "further educate"
such a dwarf ruler due to his clinical limitations, as a rule, is not possible. All,
outwardly looking like good intentions of such a worthless ruler, turn out, in
the final analysis, to be just a cover for the manifestation of private property
instincts, petty deeds and self-serving interests of the oligarchic-plutocratic
environment, which serves for the caricature ruler as a kind of "airbag".
It is amusing to watch how an ordinary figure, after the insignificant
sycophantic entourage "blows" into his ears about his non-ordinariness and
exclusiveness, suddenly begins to claim the role of a large-scale theorist and
teacher of the nation, practically not understanding the "sublime matters",
looking down with disdain and hostility at the past of the country, leveling
and calling into question what was created by truly great predecessors
(during the years of Soviet power and under the leadership of the Bolsheviks
hated by him). It is surprising how a "ruler" with an inadequate assessment
of the phenomenal past of his people can throw dust in the eyes of his fellow
citizens for so long.
In contrast to today's "leaders" and "rulers", the Bolsheviks (Lenin's closest
comrades) evoke sympathy not only due to their education, erudition, lively
mind, sober views of the world, but also thanks to iron will ("one could make
nails from these people — there would be no stronger nails in the world"),
romanticism (albeit naive to some extent), unwavering faith in the future, in
man, in his creative potential.
The Bolsheviks from the pleiad of Lenin's closest comrades selflessly, at the
cost of their freedom, health, and in many cases their lives, — managed to
break through a gap in such a thickness of millennial human ignorance,
deception and violence against ordinary people that it is simply impossible to
reassess their contribution to the formation of a new worldview (world
outlook and world order) and, therefore, one can admire them endlessly.

 As for Lenin (as a politician and statesman), the decisions made by him and
the actions performed by him must always and first of all be considered in
the context of those tasks and problems that in those times, without
exaggeration, simply "took by the throat". To understand the logic of
decisions and behavior of great politicians, one must consider this behavior
and decisions in accordance with the events and circumstances, conditions
and realities that, like a certain spatial environment or atmosphere, fill those
or other times.
By the way, modern political wretches, as already noted above ("true
democrats" — by their own standards), for the sake of preserving their
power or at the slightest threat to this power of theirs (as a rule, even in
insignificant in historicism circumstances) easily use the power appropriated
by them for the isolation or elimination of dissenters and freethinkers.
One must possess the true "greatness" and "enormity" of Lenin's nature to
leave after himself such scanty autobiographical information from personal
life, preferences, hobbies, etc. — unlike our current "rulers" striving to
immortalize (with the help of court "chroniclers") and capture on film or "in
digits" (in the form of a cinematic epic of insignificant episodes) every step of
their feigned path under the pharisaic slogan "all life is service to the
people"].
9. "Undoubtedly, the most important question of any revolution," V.I. Lenin
begins his article "One of the Fundamental Questions of the Revolution"
[9, pp. 208-214], dated September 1917. — is the question of state power;
everything is determined by the class in whose hands the power is: one
cannot bypass or postpone the question of power, for this is the fundamental
question determining everything in the development of the revolution, in its
foreign and internal policy. However, the revolution has lost half a year due
to the hesitation of the parties of the Socialist-Revolutionaries and the
Mensheviks, who are the avant-garde of the petty bourgeoisie with its
economic instability in the struggle between labor and capital. If in these
great half-years the petty-bourgeois democracy has learned anything, then it
is necessary to immediately create a stable unhesitating power; if not, then
the revolution has perished, and only the victorious uprising of the proletariat
can save it" [9, p. 208].
Only the power of the Soviets can be stable, deliberately relying on the
majority of the people, no matter how the lackeys of the bourgeoisie lie. Only
Soviet power could be stable and could ensure the broad development of the
revolution and the peaceful struggle of parties within the Soviets. Until such
power is created, indecision, hesitation, endless "crises of power", a comedy
of ministerial reshuffles are inevitable. But the slogan "All Power to the
Soviets" is often understood completely incorrectly in the sense of "a ministry
from the parties of the Soviet majority". In the indicated sense — this is just
a change in the composition of ministers while preserving the entire old
apparatus of government power, incapable of carrying out serious reforms.

 In fact, "All Power to the Soviets" means a radical reworking of the entire old
state bureaucratic apparatus that hinders everything democratic, the
elimination of this apparatus and its replacement by a new, people's
apparatus of the Soviets, i.e. the organized and armed majority of the
people, workers, soldiers, peasants, providing the initiative and
independence to the majority of the people not only in the election of
deputies, but also in governing the state, in carrying out reforms and
transformations [9, pp. 209-210].
The entire history of bourgeois-parliamentary and bourgeois-constitutional
countries, Lenin reminds, shows that a change of ministers means very little,
for the real work of management is in the hands of a gigantic army of
officials, which is thoroughly imbued with an anti-democratic spirit, is
connected by millions of threads with the bourgeoisie and is dependent on it.
This army is connected by relations of rank worship, known privileges of
"state" service, and the upper ranks of this army through the mediation of
shares and banks are completely enslaved by financial capital, representing
its agents, conductors of its interests and influence. [Isn't it somehow
"peculiarly fresh" sounding today!]. To carry out reforms to limit the right of
capital and the right of "sacred private property", such a state apparatus is
absolutely incapable [9, p. 210]. It was so and it will be so as long as the
bourgeois system holds and the old, bourgeois, bureaucratic, state apparatus
remains inviolable. The Soviets of workers', soldiers', peasants' deputies are
valuable precisely in that they represent a new, immeasurably higher,
incomparably more democratic type of state apparatus [9, p. 211]. Here
Lenin calls for not being afraid of the initiative and independence of the
masses, who are capable of revolutionary transformations and replacing the
old state apparatus.
Experience has shown that there is no middle ground: either all power to the
Soviets both in the center and on the local level, or the landlords and
capitalists hinder everything and restore their power. The situation in Russia
is such that the unprecedented hardships and misfortunes of war, the
formidable danger of collapse and hunger themselves suggested a way out
and put forward as urgent reforms and transformations: the bread monopoly,
control over production and distribution, limiting the issue of paper money,
the correct exchange of bread for goods, etc. The only class that can show
the courage and decisiveness that is lacking today is the proletariat; at the
same time, the establishment of a firm course for reforms is impossible
without the establishment of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
And, finally, the brilliant Lenin's conclusion: "Only the dictatorship of the
proletarians and the poorest peasants is able to break the resistance of the
capitalists, show truly majestic courage and decisiveness of power, ensure
for itself enthusiastic, selfless, truly heroic support of the masses both in the
army and in the peasantry" [9, p. 214]. The only thing that could make
further development gradual, peaceful and calm is the transfer of power to
the Soviets, which would mean the transfer of management of the country

 and the economy to the workers and peasants, whom no one would dare to
resist and who would quickly learn from experience to correctly distribute
land, products, bread.
[So, again we return to the initial, revealed in the course of Lenin's analysis
of the situation relation of component-classes {proletariat/bourgeoisie}, by
the interaction of components in which some of their correlation is realized,
demonstrating the supremacy, priority or prevalence of one component in
relation to another (which determines the power of one class over another).
The relation {proletariat/bourgeoisie}, filled with new content, in the form of
the transformed, transformed relation {Councils of workers', peasants' and
soldiers' deputies / bourgeois Provisional Government} shows the ability of
development (displacement) of this relation towards the "upper" component
(the "numerator"), which corresponds to the strengthening of its activity,
initiative and readiness for revolutionary transformations, to the perception
and mastery of new forms of management, productive forces, social
production, etc., etc., and which, in turn, determines the acceleration of
the contentful development of the entire relation as a whole. The emergence
of a new correlation of class forces to a new level of contentfulness (in the
form of a new relation) — this is what the Socialist-Revolutionary and
Menshevik leaders are afraid of. Again, the disruption of reforms by the
bourgeoisie is the result of inactivity or lack of sufficient control over the
situation on the part of the revolutionary component. The full development of
the indicated relation as a whole is predicted by the transfer of power to the
Soviets due to the readiness of the revolutionary popular masses for this.
In the same way, in modern conditions, without tough measures and a
revolutionary approach to solving the most urgent state tasks, one cannot do
without, no matter how hard one tries and no matter how one "blurs" the
eyes of one's fellow citizens. If the current "ruler" hopes that everything will
resolve itself, he is deeply mistaken in this regard — women have not yet
learned to give birth to such oligarchs, magnates, majors and other
"appropriators" who would voluntarily renounce what was earned in the
sweat of someone else's face and in favor of their own face appropriated. It
is a pity, nevertheless, that the current "governor" is not a resolute
revolutionary.
The reverse side of any revolution, and then counter-revolution, is (along
with class wars and squabbles) the settlement of personal, family, shop,
corporate and other scores; at the same time, the following semantic chain is
approximately realized: revenge => retribution => compensation =>
restoration of equilibrium (balance), i.e. justice... (the very etymology of
words builds them into a similar semantic chain, corresponding to the
direction of the course of processes of dialectical development). This is the
external manifestation of the dialectical nature of developing reality in the
field of human relations. At the "higher" levels — this is a contest of
competing concepts and ideologies; at more "down-to-earth" levels — this is

 a physical (force) struggle, conditioned by the desire (thirst) for the
restoration of trampled justice, violated property (household) equilibrium.
The mentioned chain can be clothed in a more attractive form, i.e. somehow
ennoble, put on the clothes of legal laws, but it will never be possible to
eradicate or abolish this chain, since in its depth, in essence — this is the
same engine of contentful renewal, progress, development.]
10. The letter "The Bolsheviks Must Take Power" [9, pp. 325-327],
addressed to the Central, Petrograd and Moscow Committees of the
RSDLP(b), was written in September 1917. Here Lenin emphasizes that,
having received a majority in both metropolitan Soviets of Workers' and
Soldiers' Deputies, the Bolsheviks can and must take state power into their
own hands. Having an active majority of the people (sufficient to break the
enemy's resistance), proposing a democratic peace, giving the land to the
peasants immediately, restoring the democratic freedoms trampled by the
Kerensky government, the Bolsheviks will form such a government that no
one will overthrow. One must not be deceived by the figures of elections to
city dumas: only elections to the Soviets show the true, truthful correlation
of forces (i.e. of components in the established relation-form {Soviets of
Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies / bourgeois Provisional Government}) at the
present moment. The people are tired of the hesitation of the Mensheviks
and Socialist-Revolutionaries, and only the victory of the Bolsheviks in both
capitals will draw the peasants after the Bolsheviks. Thus, the agenda should
include questions about the armed uprising in Petrograd and Moscow, the
conquest of power and the overthrow of the Provisional Government. In this
regard, Lenin very aptly quotes Engels' words about the uprising:
"Insurrection is an art" [17, p. 100].
"Having taken power at once in Moscow and Petrograd... we will win
unconditionally and undoubtedly," Lenin concludes [9, p. 327].
[The establishment and "fixity" of a new correlation between the components
in the notorious relation-form {Soviets / Provisional Government} (i.e. the
statement of the fact of the majority of the people on the side of the Soviets)
gives grounds for the conclusion about the relevance and legitimacy of a
non-violent transition and transfer of all state power into the hands of the
Soviets. A correctly performed assessment of the achieved correlation
between the mentioned components in their established relation allows one
to confidently forecast the course of the uprising and count on its most
peaceful and bloodless outcome].
11. Another letter of Lenin to the Central Committee of the RSDLP(b) (known
as an article under the title "Marxism and Insurrection" [9, pp. 328-332]
and written approximately on the same days as the previous letter) was a
reaction to the accusations of the Bolsheviks' adherence to the ideas of
"Blanquism". These accusations arose on the basis of the Bolsheviks' attitude
to the uprising as to an art (absolutizing allegedly the role of the subjective

 beginning, which is characteristic of Blanquism, based, as is known, on the
theory of conspiracies and terror).
Meanwhile, it was Marxism, according to Lenin, that called the uprising an
art, explaining that the uprising must be treated as an art: to win the first
success and from success to go to success, without ceasing the offensive
against the enemy, taking advantage of his confusion and indecision, etc.
Fighting the accusations of Blanquism, Lenin determines the three main
signs-conditions of success [i.e. of achieving the highest contentfulness by
the forms-relations participating in the revolutionary process] of the uprising:
firstly, reliance on the advanced class; secondly, reliance on the
revolutionary upsurge of the people; thirdly, reliance on such a turning point
in the history of the growing revolution when the greatest activity of the
people is accompanied by the strongest fluctuations in the ranks of the
enemies and indecisive "friends" of the revolution. "It is by these three
conditions of posing the question of the uprising that Marxism differs from
Blanquism," Lenin concludes [9, p. 328].
To prove the urgent necessity of the uprising from the point of view of the
objective agenda, and not subjective conjectures, Vladimir Ilyich traces the
change of objective conditions, the situation in the period of time from July
to September of the same 1917, trying to identify the trend or direction of
such changes. In July, in his firm conviction, the above-mentioned
indispensable conditions for the success of the uprising were not yet
observed, while by September the general picture had changed radically and
now "all objective prerequisites for a successful uprising are evident" [9, p.
330]. Victory in the uprising, in Lenin's opinion, will disrupt Kerensky's game
with the surrender of Petrograd and the conclusion of a separate peace with
Germany against the revolution and will ensure the conclusion of a more
complete, open, fair peace in favor of the revolution. Only the Bolshevik
party, having won in the uprising, can save Petrograd from surrender to the
Germans and save the whole of Russia from the separate division by the
imperialists of both warring coalitions. The Bolsheviks must draw up a short
declaration, insisting on the necessity of immediate actions for the sake of
saving the revolution, the necessity of a complete break with the bourgeoisie,
the complete removal of the current government, the complete break with
the Anglo-French imperialists preparing a separate division of Russia, the
necessity of an immediate transfer of all power into the hands of the
revolutionary democracy led by the revolutionary proletariat. The short and
sharp declaration must contain two most important points: 1) the people are
tired of the hesitation and indecision of the Socialist-Revolutionaries and
Mensheviks and therefore breaks with these parties finally, for they have
betrayed the revolution; 2) a break with the allied imperialists and a proposal
for peace without annexations lead either to an immediate truce or to the
transition of the revolutionary proletariat to defense and waging a truly fair
revolutionary war under its leadership. Having published the declaration, the
Bolsheviks must put their entire faction forward to the factories and barracks

 — that is its place, there is the nerve of life, there is the source of salvation
of the revolution. Posing the question in this way, the Bolsheviks will be able
to correctly appoint the moment of the beginning of the uprising, having
previously organized the headquarters of the rebel detachments, mobilized
the armed workers for a desperate last decisive battle, occupied the
telegraph, telephone and connected all factories, all regiments, all points of
armed struggle with the headquarters, etc. [9, pp. 331-332].
[Thus, the transfer of accents and the shift of the correlation of components
in the known relations towards more contentful, active and active
components and thereby bringing these relations to the form {Soviets (under
the aegis of the Bolsheviks) / Provisional Government (in alliance with the
bourgeoisie and foreign financial capital)} changes the entire tactics of the
Bolsheviks in the conditions of the growing revolutionary movement. In other
words, speaking in everyday language, the first revolution of the proletariat,
the peasantry and the bourgeoisie in alliance with the Anglo-French financial
capital against tsarism before our eyes is growing into a revolution of the
proletariat and the poorest peasantry against the bourgeoisie with its ally the
Anglo-French financial capital and the Kerensky government].
As has already been shown earlier, a similar schematically-described above
plot construction can be seen in almost all of Lenin's theoretical works. Thus,
we have some grounds for building and formulating a methodology (or even
a whole methodology) for researching the perspective of the movementdevelopment-change of the forms-relations of interacting components in
different areas and at different levels of reality.
12. The article "On Compromises" [9, pp. 158-163] was printed on
September 19, 1917 in connection with the opened opportunity for the
Bolsheviks to conclude a voluntary compromise with a number of other
parties.
"A compromise," Lenin writes, "is called in politics the concession of some
demands, the renunciation of part of one's demands by virtue of an
agreement with another party" [9, p. 158]. The usual idea of the Bolsheviks
was that the Bolsheviks do not agree with anyone and never on any
compromises. Such an idea is flattering, for even enemies are forced to
recognize the party of the revolutionary proletariat's fidelity to the principles
of socialism and revolution. However, to tell the truth, such an idea does not
correspond to the truth. The task of a truly revolutionary party consists not
in not succumbing to compromises, but in being able, through all
compromises, to maintain fidelity to its principles, fidelity to its class, its
cause of preparing the revolution and the corresponding education of the
masses.
The Bolshevik party, like any other, strives for political domination for itself
in the name of achieving its goal; the immediate goal for the Bolsheviks is
the establishment of the dictatorship of the revolutionary proletariat. And

 yet, in the current conditions of the original turn of the Russian revolution,
the Bolsheviks (as a party) can offer a voluntary compromise, however, not
to the bourgeoisie (i.e. the main class enemy), but to the SocialistRevolutionaries and Mensheviks (the dominant petty-bourgeois democratic
parties). Now within a very short period of time it is possible to return to the
slogan "All Power to the Soviets"; at the same time, the government
responsible to the Soviets will consist of the Socialist-Revolutionaries and
Mensheviks. Such a combined variant could ensure with a gigantic probability
the peaceful movement forward of the entire Russian revolution and
extremely high chances of the worldwide movement towards peace and the
victory of socialism. "Only in the name of this peaceful development of
the revolution — an opportunity, extremely rare in history and extremely
valuable, an opportunity, exceptionally rare, only in its name the Bolsheviks,
supporters of the world revolution, supporters of revolutionary methods, can
and must, in my opinion, go for such a compromise" [9, p. 159].
[And again Lenin, as a true dialectician, discovers a certain new (capable of
functioning effectively) relation of components {Soviets / government of
Socialist-Revolutionaries and Mensheviks}, the correlation of which at that
given particular moment would contribute to giving an additional impetus to
the prospective revolutionary movement].
But such an outcome was possible at the moment Lenin was preparing this
article. However, literally a couple of days later, the situation began to
change rapidly and the events that occurred showed that the proposal for a
compromise was already late; the few days during which peaceful
development would still have been possible had passed. It became obvious
that due to the inaction of the Socialist-Revolutionaries, the favorable "days
when the road of peaceful development became possible by chance, have
already passed" [9, p. 163].
13. The article "An Outsider's Tips" [9, pp. 391-393] was written on the
eve of the Great October Socialist Revolution. The current situation makes it
clear that in the conditions of the greatest sympathy and support for the
revolutionary-proletarian (Bolshevik) power on the part of all workers and
exploited people in the world in general, and in the warring countries in
particular, and among the Russian peasantry in particular — all Bolsheviks
should be quite clear: the transfer of power to the Soviets now means in
practice an armed uprising. To renounce the armed uprising is tantamount to
renouncing the main slogan of Bolshevism — "All Power to the Soviets". And
here Vladimir Ilyich again insists on the well-known Marxist thesis: "Armed
uprising, like war, is an art" [9, p. 391]. Marxism formulates the following
main rules of this art: 1) having started the uprising, one must firmly go to
the end; 2) in the decisive place and at the decisive moment, it is necessary
to gather a large superiority of forces; 3) defense is the death of an armed
uprising — one must necessarily go over to the offensive; 4) one must try to
take the enemy by surprise; 5) to achieve small successes daily and move
from success to success, maintaining at all costs the "moral superiority".

 In the adaptation of these general rules to the specific situation, Lenin
highlights the following points: 1) the organization of a sudden and rapid
offensive on Petrograd both from within and from outside with the aim of
creating a gigantic superiority of forces, paralyzing the response actions of
the Junkers, and thereby achieving the bloodlessness ("low-bloodedness") of
the uprising; 2) by the three main revolutionary forces (the fleet, workers
and military units) the main objects must be taken under control and held at
any cost: telephone, telegraph, bridges, railway stations; 3) the formation of
small detachments from the most resolute and steadfast comrades, ready to
provide operational support in the most important directions.
[Here we see that without any reservations or delays, Lenin finally bets on
the new correlation of components and the superiority of the "Soviets"
component (i.e. the predominance of the "numerator" over the
"denominator") that had developed by that time in the relation {Soviets /
Provisional Government} and on this basis plans the success and the
acquisition of a new quality by the indicated relation in its transformation into
a more contentful and prospective form.]
According to the circumstances that had developed then, Lenin believed that
"the success of the Russian and world revolution depends on two or three
days of struggle" [9, p. 393].
§ 3. Works of the post-revolutionary period
The Great October Socialist Revolution has been accomplished. The
Bolsheviks took power, but it did not become calmer or simpler. The agenda
includes new topical questions: how to hold power, how to suppress the
resistance of the counter-revolution, how to move on to building a peaceful
life, how to awaken the creative initiative of the masses, etc.
1. In the article "Speech on the Nationalization of Banks at the Meeting
of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee on December 27,
1917. Protocol Record" [9, pp. 462-464], published on December 29,
1917, it is about the opposition of the new power of the Soviets by the old
bourgeois bureaucratic apparatus. The old apparatus with all its might tries
to present the banking issue as extremely fragile, complex and confusing, in
order to maximally slow down the process of transferring affairs into the
hands of representatives of the new power and to hinder all socialist
undertakings. Regarding all decisions of the Council, they ["apparatchiks"]
declare that they agree, but only in principle. The entire system of bourgeois
intelligentsia, in Lenin's opinion, is distinguished by "its constant agreement
in principle and disagreement in practice", which ruins the whole cause [9,
p. 462].
From the very first days, the new power faces opposition, when its decisive
steps are approved in theory and nothing but sabotage is met in practice. No
one (except utopian socialists) had previously claimed that it is possible to

 win without resistance and without establishing the dictatorship of the
proletariat; and this fundamental point was not disputed by anyone. But
when the word "dictatorship" is translated into Russian and its equivalent
"iron hand" is reached, then all the former zeal disappears somewhere and
lamentations begin about the fragility and confusion of the issue [all the
pressure is suddenly leveled and nullified by referring to the complexity and
confusion of issues]. However, here one must see that this iron hand,
destroying, also creates.
After all, at first there was talk of an agreement with the banks ("who wants
to work — you are welcome"), they were issued loans for financing
enterprises, but they started sabotage of an unprecedented size, and practice
led the Bolsheviks to exercise control by other measures. Now the words
"dictatorship of the proletariat" are spoken by the Bolsheviks very seriously,
and this dictatorship will be implemented.
2. And then, on the hot heels, “A draft decree ["road map", as they would
say today] on the implementation of the nationalization of banks and
the necessary measures in connection with this” was created and
submitted by Lenin for discussion by the bureau of the Supreme Council of
the National Economy [9, pp. 465-467], which determined the direction of
movement and transformations of the banking sector for the near future and
many years to come. Delay with the approval of the decree was already
tantamount to the disruption of the entire economy due to the powerful
opposition and sabotage on the part of the banks.
In the preamble to the mentioned Draft Decree [9, p. 465], it is said about
the critical food situation and the threat of famine generated by the
speculation and sabotage of capitalists and officials, which leads to the need
to take extraordinary revolutionary measures to combat this evil. So that all
citizens of the state and, first of all, the working classes under the leadership
of their Soviets of workers', soldiers' and peasants' deputies could
immediately, "stopping at nothing and acting in the most revolutionary way,
take up such a struggle and the establishment of the correct economic life of
the country, the following rules are established", which are further set out in
the body of the Draft Decree [below are the rules that, in our opinion, are of
the greatest interest to us today from the point of view of their continued
effectiveness to this day.]

All joint-stock enterprises are declared the property of the state.
All shareholders "belonging to the rich classes" are obliged to continue
managing the affairs of enterprises, providing weekly reports on their activities
to the local Soviets.
Government loans (external and internal) are annulled, but the interests
of small owners of bonds (as well as shares) belonging to the working classes of
the population are fully secured.

Universal labor conscription is introduced, when all citizens of both
sexes, from 16 to 55 years old, are obliged to perform work assigned by the
local Soviets.
For correct accounting and distribution of food and other essential
products, all citizens of the state are obliged to join some consumer society and
perform the work that will be imposed on them by the Soviets.
Unions of railway workers and employees are obliged to urgently
develop and immediately begin to implement emergency measures to provide
transport, especially for the delivery of food, fuel and other essential items. The
duty of waging a merciless struggle against speculators is also imposed on them.
"Persons of the rich classes" are obliged to keep all their money sums in
the State Bank, its branches and savings banks, receiving for consumer needs
the sums established by the local Soviets; sums for production and trade needs
can be obtained only with written certificates from worker control institutions;
"those guilty of deceiving the state and the people will be subject to confiscation
of all property".
"The same punishment, as well as imprisonment or sending to the front
and to forced labor, is subject to all disobedient to this law, saboteurs and
striking officials, as well as speculators. The local Soviets... are obliged to
urgently develop the most revolutionary measures of struggle against these real
enemies of the people."
Trade unions and other organizations of workers in conjunction with the
local Soviets organize flying groups of controllers from the most reliable and
recommended by party organizations persons to monitor the implementation of
this law, to check the quantity and quality of work and to bring to revolutionary
courts those guilty of violating or circumventing the law.
"Workers and employees of nationalized enterprises are obliged to strain
all forces and take emergency measures to improve the organization of work,
strengthen discipline, increase labor productivity. The bodies of worker control
must provide weekly reports on what has been achieved in this regard. For
shortcomings and omissions, the guilty are answerable before the revolutionary
court" [9, p. 467].
[And again the contradictory question requires a solution — finding the correct
correlation of components-constituents in the relation {dictatorship of the
proletariat / soft government apparatus of indecisive bourgeois intelligentsia}.
The "iron hand" or the dictatorship of the proletariat is precisely that rigorous
accounting and control over production and distribution, which must be strictly
exercised not only in wartime conditions, but throughout the entire period of
socialist construction, until the principles of morality, ethics, honest attitude to
work enter the blood and flesh of every person — both at the level of conscious
perception and at the level of the subconscious. The tricks of bourgeois games
described in the article were revealed by the Bolsheviks in the first months of the
functioning of Soviet power, which is why decisions were made to act in
response quite harshly and immediately, so that the previous sacrifices and
efforts would not be in vain.]

 3. In the article "How to Organize Competition?" [9, pp. 468-476], written in
January 1918, the conditions for awakening genuine competition to life, as well
as the initiative of the masses, are considered.
Already at the dawn of the emergence of capitalist relations, the competition of
small commodity producers could on a somewhat wide scale educate enterprise,
energy, the boldness of initiative; in fact, today capitalism has replaced small
independent production with the largest factory production, joint-stock
enterprises, syndicates and other monopolies. Competition in this layout means,
on the contrary, the suppression of the enterprise of the mass of the population,
the replacement of competition with financial fraud and servility to the "tops" of
the social ladder [9, p. 468]. [How amazingly accurately and fairly this "sounds"
in relation to the rampage of the wildest capitalism in modern Russia and in the
post-Soviet space!].
To develop abilities, to reveal human talents (which the people have in
abundance) on a mass scale is possible only with a properly organized socialist
method of production. The most urgent task today, when the socialist
government is in power, is to organize competition.
[It is striking how from the very first days of Soviet power, in the conditions of
an economic chaos, collapse, and famine that have not yet been overcome,
Lenin thinks in categories of the most peaceful and calm time, in categories of
education and formation of new production relations between workers,
awakening the initiative of people on a "mass scale"!].
"A broad, truly mass creation of the opportunity to show enterprise, competition,
a bold initiative is only now. ...For the first time after centuries of work for
others, forced work for exploiters, the opportunity to work for oneself arises, and
moreover work based on all the achievements of the latest technology and
culture" [9, p. 469].
It is quite clear that the greatest change in history of mankind from forced labor
to labor for oneself cannot occur without conflicts, without overcoming the
resistance of exploiters, without displacing the capitalists, which will take time.
In addition to the "military" measures of suppressing the resistance of the "rich
classes", the proletariat and the poorest peasantry will also need huge
organizational efforts. Thus, the organizational task is intertwined with the task
of ruthless military suppression of yesterday's slave owners (capitalists and their
lackeys — the gentlemen of the bourgeois intelligentsia).
Naturally, none of the past "masters of life" wants to voluntarily part with their
former command and "bread" privileged posts, considering themselves "Godchosen" patrons and managers over the people. "But the matter of the exploiters
and their intellectual lackeys is a hopeless matter." Their resistance, workers and
peasants will eventually break decisively and ruthlessly.

 Intellectuals accustomed to serving capitalists and the capitalist state believe
that they cannot be done without. "Their impudent calculation will not be
justified: educated people are already standing out, going over to the side of the
people, to the side of the workers, helping to break the resistance of the
servants of capital. And there are many organizational talents in the peasantry
and the working class, and these talents are just beginning to realize
themselves, to wake up, to reach for living, creative, great work, to take up the
construction of a socialist society independently" [9, p. 470].
Perhaps the most important task today, Lenin says, is to develop as widely as
possible the independent initiative of workers in the matter of creative
organizational work. It is necessary to break the vile and absurd prejudice that
only the so-called "higher classes" and only the rich can manage the
organizational construction of society. Organizational work is "within the power
of an ordinary worker and peasant who has literacy, knowledge of people,
practical experience. ...There is still an inexhaustible spring and a richest spring
of such talents in the working class and in the peasantry." Workers and peasants
are still timid, they have not yet got used to the fact that they are now the ruling
class. But the strength and vitality of the October Revolution of 1917 lies in the
fact that it leads the working people to the path of independent creation of a new
life.
[For the note of the current "rulers" and their ilk: Lenin in a matter of years
found ways from scratch to motivate the illiterate, bast-shod population of the
bloodless country, and the current "ruler" with his "valiant" arrogant entourage
has been struggling for several terms (both in a row and intermittently) to solve
the same task, but in vain.
The conservative "comprador" entourage of the current "ruler" will not allow him
(the ruler) to make a single decision encroaching on the self-serving interest of
this entourage. So all this pompous camarilla will sit and wait for mythical
Western investments like manna from heaven, shifting the blame for their failure
on the notorious Western sanctions. Fortunately, their own fortunes are reliably
placed in foreign lands with the hope that such ugliness will continue forever.
For the information of today's "rulers": Lenin, in the five or six years granted
to him after the revolution, managed (in the conditions of discord and
devastation, having tried many options) to find ways to awaken both
enthusiasm and the initiative of millions, and to attract foreign specialists,
and to train and prepare his own... Human potential (physical strength,
intellectual and spiritual energy of the people) — this is the source of all
investments, technologies and innovations, and therefore the main
component of the country's economic success; however, the inept
"comprador" entourage of the supreme "ruler" will skillfully, on the verge of
sabotage, extinguish this potential and write off all failures to the lack of
overseas investments and the omnipotence of overseas sanctions.
By the way, has the main "ruler" tried to pull "overseas investments" out of
the purse of his entourage?

 Regarding the liberal-minded (in relation to the aggressive collective West)
circles in Russia, it is somehow already old-fashioned, unpleasant, and not
desirable to speak. Since the words of F.M. Dostoevsky, it has been known
that "our Russian liberal is first and foremost a lackey and only looks for how
to clean someone's boots" [4, p. 133]. Meanwhile, eternal kneeling before
the West is conditioned by the universality and generality of the very
principle of self-development.
The aspiration of all forms to the highest contentfulness has an unsightly
reverse side in the imposition (as a sample or standard) of its allegedly
most perfect and exclusive form — its understanding of the world, its
ideology (with the accompanying "uprooting" of dissent and everything
"wrong"), its worldview, world outlook, world perception, its way of life —

 more Contentful views: principles of human morality, ethics, spirituality,

At the same time, implementing socialist undertakings, the Soviets of
workers', soldiers' and peasants' deputies, consumer societies, supply
unions, factory committees and worker control bodies must understand that
the main economic task at this stage is accounting and control. The old
habit of a forced person is still strong — as if to "grab" at least a piece from
the bourgeoisie, without burdening oneself with extra work and obligations.
Such an approach of "newcomers" to the factory environment: "Grab a
bigger piece and run away", — is transferred to the factory that has passed
into the ownership of the people. The advanced conscious workers have
already started fighting against such personnel, who will undoubtedly be
supported by honest, thinking peasants. Universal, universal, universal
accounting and control over the distribution of products and the amount of
labor — this is the essence of the socialist transformation; the accounting
and control necessary for the transition to socialism can only be mass.
Proceeding from this, Lenin turns to the new working owners of land, banks,
factories and plants: "Take up the accounting and control of production and
distribution yourselves, — this is the only way to the victory of socialism, the
pledge of its victory, the pledge of victory over all exploitation, over all need
and poverty". In Russia, Lenin says, there is enough bread, iron, forest,
wool, cotton and flax for everyone, if a nationwide businesslike, practical
control over distribution is established, if the enemies of the people (the rich
and their "hangers-on" — bourgeois intellectuals) are defeated not only in
politics, but also in the everyday economic life of a society in which "a
handful robbed the people and mocked the people" [9, p. 472]. [An
extremely topical appeal also applicable to the current situation in Russia!].
"The rich and crooks, these are two sides of the same coin, these are the two
main categories of parasites fostered by capitalism, these are the main
enemies of socialism, these enemies must be placed under the special
supervision of the entire population, they must be dealt with, at the slightest
violation by them of the rules and laws of socialist society, mercilessly. Any
weakness, any hesitation, any sentimentality in this regard would be the
greatest crime against socialism" [9, p. 473].
[If only Lenin with his dialectical mind were here, even for an hour !!!

 Our great Motherland has again been turned into a country of lackeys and
masters, where a handful of plutocrats does at an unconscious level
everything that comes to mind, satisfying primarily their primitive
momentary whims and fancies, dictated only by the desire to increase their
own savings, thereby determining and setting in advance, for years, the
configuration of our (or rather, their) future and without our participation in
this. Before, such a thing could not even be dreamed of or seen in a
nightmare. Lenin's lessons of dialectics have turned out to be, at
best, Unlearned lessons of dialectics.]
The way to neutralize these parasites is a nationwide, organized by millions
of workers and peasants, voluntary and energetic accounting and control
over the amount of labor, production and distribution of products. And in
order to organize this accounting and control, which is quite accessible and
feasible for every honest, sensible and efficient worker and peasant, it is
necessary to call their own organizational talents to life, it is necessary to
establish on an all-state scale a competition in terms of organizational
successes, it is necessary that workers and peasants clearly understand the
difference between the necessary advice of an educated person and the
necessary control of a simple worker and peasant over the sloppiness, so
common among educated people.
Sloppiness, carelessness, untidiness, "the tendency to take on everything in
the world and bring nothing to an end is one of the properties of "educated
people", stemming not at all from their bad nature, much less from malice,
but from all the habits of life, from the setting of their work, from overwork",
from the abnormal correlation of the mental and physical components of
labor in the cycles of their activity, etc., etc.
[And here we see a surprisingly insightful and precise statement of the
connection between the actual mistakes, shortcomings and misses made
during the revolution and those "sad, but inevitable" at that moment abovementioned "properties of intellectuals", as well as the lack of sufficient
control from the workers over the organizational work of intellectuals. Most
of all, hesitation and indecision, which are so characteristic of the
intelligentsia and which the intelligentsia is guilty of, are unacceptable to
Lenin.
Any hesitation after the adoption of a collective decision was tantamount to
betrayal and defeat for Lenin. Ilyich is always tuned and charged for victory.
The same applies to compromises (namely in relation to his ideological
opponents), to which the bourgeois intelligentsia is most inclined, being weak
in spirit (i.e. not having fundamental ideological convictions). Lenin also
includes here the desire to sit on two chairs; nowadays — this is the
notorious political "multi-vector". Indecision and hesitation, in the end, often
turn into extra unnecessary victims; these are those absurd mistakes that
could have been avoided by adhering to a firm position. The enemy is like an
uncomfortable hard, but "firm ground", and the wavering and indecisive

 "fellow traveler" is akin to a swamp: try to know when it will "absorb" and
"digest" you, i.e. simply betray.
In modern Russia, the role of the petty-bourgeois wavering conciliators with
those in power is played by "pocket" parties and groups like modern
centrists, communists, liberals of all names, etc., with a vague position —
declassed elements, dangling somewhere "between here and between
there"; the place of the actual spokesman for the opinions of the working
class of wage workers remains vacant as before. In general, regarding the
betrayal and apostasy of the intelligentsia, when the cause of a whole life is
threatened, anyone would speak even more harshly and emotionally than
Vladimir Ilyich does.
As in the times of V.I. Lenin, modern political and economic literature is full
of all kinds of absurdities: and some "middle class" was invented, and
ownership of the means of production no longer has any significance, and a
two-party system is strictly obligatory for progress, etc. If you come to think
of it, any person always has an internal content-form (i.e. at least twocomponent, two-sided, dual) contradiction, which serves as the engine of all
progress and development even more fiercely than the contest, competition
or conflict of two or several parties; in one person, opposing components can
be observed and coexist, giving such an impulse of activity that no parties
are needed at all.
As they say in Russia: "In Russia there is still one party — it is just called
differently." However, something similar is observed in other countries. For
example, in the USA, liberals and conservatives (Democrats and Republicans)
have long been fighting for power only for the sake of protecting and
increasing the property and income of the propertied class. In addition, one
must always be prepared for the fact that over time the "bourgeoisification"
of the most advanced and progressive parties at first occurs due to the
degeneration of the top and part of the members of these parties into their
opposites — such is the dialectical nature of reality: one just needs to recall
this more often and shake up (clean out, as Lenin said) the party ranks.
As in the times of Lenin's pre-revolutionary political activity, today, to curb
the threat of stratification and radicalization of society, the bourgeoisie
sometimes try to integrate the topmost layers of the left and anarchists into
their system, recruit them into their ranks (having bought them off with an

the social sphere, etc.).
What kind of opposition is it in parliament if it consists of the power-fed
representatives of the same "bourgeoisified" class as the official propertied
ruling class? Where does the dividing line pass between the official power
and the systemic alleged opposition, among the leading members of which
the owners and co-owners (shareholders) of "factories, newspapers,
steamships" with assets placed outside the borders of our Motherland
suddenly find themselves by chance?]

 develop on the issues of eliminating hunger, unemployment, eradicating the
